paragraphs.heading: What astronomy studies
paragraphs.text: Astronomy is the natural science of the objects found in space and of the events that happen out there. In its widest sense, it covers anything that comes from beyond Earth's atmosphere. The objects include planets, moons, stars, nebulae, galaxies, asteroids, comets and meteoroids. Among the events it covers are pulsars, quasars, blazars, gamma-ray bursts, supernova explosions and the cosmic microwave background radiation. One branch, cosmology, looks at the universe taken as a single whole.

paragraphs.heading: Astronomy and astrophysics
paragraphs.text: To explain where all these things came from and how they change, astronomers lean on mathematics, physics and chemistry. Today the words astronomy and astrophysics are broadly treated as the same, and people often swap one for the other. Dictionaries do draw a fine line. Astronomy is the study of matter and objects beyond our atmosphere, including their chemical and physical properties, while astrophysics is the branch about how those objects behave and the processes that drive them.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same as astrology
paragraphs.text: The name joins two Greek words, one for star and one for law or rule. Astronomy should not be mixed up with astrology, the belief that the positions of objects in the sky are tied to human affairs. The two grew from the same roots but went separate ways. Physics supports astronomy, and it does not support astrology.

paragraphs.heading: One of the oldest sciences
paragraphs.text: Astronomy is among the oldest natural sciences. Early civilizations in recorded history, including the Egyptians, Babylonians, Greeks, Indians, Chinese and Maya, kept careful, methodical watch on the night sky. Much of the first push was practical, such as building calendars for farming. Even before writing, places like Stonehenge and objects like the Nebra sky disc, with symbols read as a sun, a moon and stars, show an interest in the sky. At Nabta Playa in Upper Egypt, huge stones were set in line with the rising of Sirius, which helped fix the yearly calendar for the Nile flood.

paragraphs.heading: Babylon and Greece
paragraphs.text: The Babylonians began astronomy based on mathematics, and later traditions built on their work. They found, for example, that eclipses of the Moon come back in a cycle of 223 synodic months, called the saros. Greek astronomers then looked for rational, physical reasons behind what they saw. In the 4th century BC Heracleides Ponticus proposed that Earth spins on its own axis, and a century later Aristarchus of Samos suggested that Earth and the planets go around the Sun, the idea now called the heliocentric model. In the 2nd century BC Hipparchus listed 1020 stars and invented the earliest known instruments of the field, such as the astrolabe.

paragraphs.heading: Earth at the centre
paragraphs.text: The Antikythera mechanism, made around 150 to 80 BC, was an early analog computer that worked out where the Sun, Moon and planets would be on a chosen date. Nothing as complex turned up again until mechanical astronomical clocks appeared in Europe in the 14th century. After the classical Greek era, the leading picture was the geocentric model, or Ptolemaic system, named after Claudius Ptolemy, in which Earth sat at the centre with the Sun, Moon and stars moving around it. His 13-volume work, known by the name of its Arabic translation, the Almagest, stayed the main reference for over a thousand years. The system was later thrown out, yet in its time it gave the most accurate forecasts of where objects in the sky would be.

paragraphs.heading: A science amateurs still shape
paragraphs.text: Astronomy is one of the few sciences where amateurs take an active part. This is truest for finding and watching transient events. Amateurs have played a part in many important finds, such as new comets.
